stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Ines, a nutrition scientist, is visiting her grandmother.

Ines had spent a decade counting grams of sodium for strangers, and she arrived at her grandmother's kitchen braced to disapprove. The stew was dark with salted pork; the bread had been fried in lard. She opened her mouth to say something about arteries. But her grandmother was humming as she ladled, and the neighbors crowding the table were laughing over one another, and Ines found that the lecture she had rehearsed on the train no longer seemed to belong in the room. She took a second bowl and said nothing.
choices: Ines, prepared to criticize the meal, decides that the nutritional advice she has given for years is mistaken.
Ines, prepared to criticize the meal, sets aside her objections once she experiences the warmth of the gathering.
Ines notices that her grandmother's stew and bread are made with salted pork and fried in lard.
Ines grows irritated by the noisy neighbors and decides to leave before the meal is over.
explanation: Follow Ines from start to end: she arrives 'braced to disapprove,' but after 'But' the humming grandmother and laughing neighbors make her lecture feel out of place, and she quietly takes a second bowl. Choice B gets both halves right: the situation (ready to criticize) and the direction her feeling takes (she lets the objection go because of the warmth in the room).

A.why: This is the half-right answer. The first half is accurate, but the text never says Ines thinks her science is wrong. She only decides this isn't the moment for a lecture. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

C.why: This is true, but it covers just one sentence. It leaves out Ines's change of heart, which is what the whole passage builds toward. It is too narrow.

D.why: This gets the tone backwards. The laughter wins Ines over rather than annoying her, and she stays for a second bowl instead of leaving.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires recognizing a subtle shift (prepared critique overridden by human warmth) and avoiding the trap that she rejects her expertise entirely

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker, a sports scientist, is timing a young runner on a track.

The stopwatch knows her by hundredths: / stride length, ground contact, the angle / of a knee at the moment of push. / I have charted her for three seasons, / every figure tidier than the last. / Yet this morning, when she crossed the line / and threw her head back, laughing, into the wind, / I looked down and found I had forgotten / to press the button at all.
choices: The speaker describes the precise measurements used to track the runner's stride and form.
The speaker, who has measured the runner for years, regrets an error that spoiled a season of data.
The speaker grows frustrated that the runner's times have stopped improving after three seasons.
The speaker, who has measured the runner for years, is so moved by her joy that the timing is forgotten.
explanation: Put the poem into plain English. For three seasons the speaker has recorded this runner in exact detail. Then 'Yet' brings the turn: the runner crosses the line laughing, and the speaker is so caught up in the moment that they never stop the watch. Choice D covers the years of measuring and the turn at the end.

A.why: This only describes the images in the opening lines. It skips the turn after 'Yet,' which is what the poem is really about. That is the usual poetry trap.

B.why: The first half is right, but nothing in the poem suggests regret or lost data. It misses one timing on one morning, and the tone is wonder, not dismay. Read every choice to the end.

C.why: The poem says each figure was 'tidier than the last,' so the runner is getting better, and the speaker shows delight, not frustration.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Must distinguish between regret (trap B) and emotional transformation (correct D) by noticing tone.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a short story. Priya, a public health officer, is writing the final report on a clean-water campaign she led.

The report was due Friday, and Priya had the numbers: cholera admissions down by two thirds, the new pumps working in eleven of twelve villages. The minister's office would want a photograph. She thought instead of the twelfth village, where the pump had cracked in the first frost and a woman had walked her, without complaint, to the old well her family still used. Priya typed the figures, looked at them for a long time, and then added a paragraph no one had asked for.
choices: Although the campaign largely succeeded, Priya is unwilling to leave its one failure out of her report.
Although the campaign largely succeeded, Priya worries that the minister will blame her for the broken pump.
Priya records that the new pumps are working in eleven of the twelve villages in the campaign.
Priya is pleased that her report will present the campaign to the minister as a complete success.
explanation: The last sentence ties it together. Priya has strong numbers, but her mind keeps going back to the twelfth village. After staring at the figures, she adds a paragraph 'no one had asked for,' meaning she chooses to write about the failure too. Choice A captures both the success and that choice.

B.why: This gives Priya a motive the text never mentions. Nothing suggests she is afraid of blame. She is thinking about the woman at the well. The first half is right and the second half is made up.

C.why: This is a true detail from the first sentence, but it is too narrow. It leaves out what Priya does with the numbers, which is the point of the passage.

D.why: This reverses the ending. Priya adds the paragraph because she doesn't want the report to look like a complete success.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Requires multi-step inference: understanding that unsolicited paragraph reveals Priya's integrity about the failure, not fear.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a memoir. The author, a musicologist, describes transcribing old field recordings of folk songs.

For the first month I transcribed the tapes as I had been trained to: pitch, rhythm, the placement of each ornament, all of it pinned to the staff. The singers were long dead, and the hiss of the old reels made them sound farther away still. Then, on a recording from 1958, a woman stopped mid-verse to scold a child, laughed, and began the line again a half step higher. I did not notate the change. I rewound the tape and listened to her laugh, and then I listened again.
choices: The author grows impatient with interruptions that make the old recordings difficult to transcribe.
The author's routine technical work gives way to a decision to abandon formal notation entirely.
The author's routine technical work gives way to fascination with a singer as a real person.
The author explains that one singer resumed her verse a half step higher than she began it.
explanation: Follow how the author feels over time. At first the work is mechanical and the singers seem far away. Then one woman's unplanned moment pulls the author in, and they stop notating and replay her laugh. Choice C describes that move from routine to fascination.

A.why: This gets the tone backwards. The interruption fascinates the author, who rewinds to hear it again rather than getting annoyed.

B.why: The first half is right, but the author skips notating one change on one tape. Nothing says they give up notation altogether. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

D.why: This is accurate but covers only one detail. It leaves out the author's reaction, which is what the passage is building to.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Distinguishing between abandoning notation entirely (trap B) and pausing to witness a person (correct C).

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Dr. Halloran, an archaeologist, is supervising students at a Roman-era excavation.

The students had wanted gold, and for six weeks the trench had given them only potsherds and the bones of sheep. Halloran watched their enthusiasm drain away over lunch. On the last afternoon, however, a girl from Leeds brushed the dirt from a roof tile and found, pressed into the clay before firing, the small clear print of a dog's paw. The students crowded round, suddenly silent. Halloran, who had seen a hundred such tiles, found she had no wish to tell them so.
choices: Halloran keeps the tile's commonness a secret because she fears the students will give up archaeology.
A student uncovers a roof tile bearing a dog's paw print that was pressed in before the clay was fired.
The students remain bored with the excavation even after a discovery is made on the final afternoon.
Halloran, though familiar with such finds, chooses not to spoil the students' newly awakened wonder.
explanation: After 'however,' an ordinary find leaves the discouraged students 'suddenly silent,' which here means awed. The last sentence moves to Halloran: she knows these tiles are common but has 'no wish' to tell them. Choice D matches the situation and the feeling it ends on.

A.why: This adds a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests Halloran is afraid of the students quitting. She simply doesn't want to spoil their moment.

B.why: This is true but describes only the find. It leaves out how the students and Halloran react, which is what the passage is about.

C.why: This reverses the change in tone. The students were bored earlier, but the paw print pulls them in, which is the point of the 'however.'

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Requires inferring Halloran's emotional choice to protect students' wonder over her urge to correct their awe.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker, an immunologist, is looking at blood cells under a microscope.

Under the lens they are only shapes: / the macrophage slumped like a sack of grain, / the lymphocytes small and round as seeds. / I have named them all a thousand times. / But tonight, my own blood on the slide, / I watched one cell reach out and swallow / a thing that would have harmed me, / and I thanked it, aloud, alone in the lab, / as if it could hear.
choices: The speaker compares the shapes of familiar blood cells to everyday objects such as grain and seeds.
Seeing their own cells at work turns the speaker's routine observation into personal gratitude.
Seeing their own cells at work, the speaker fears that their immune system is beginning to fail.
The speaker concludes that immunologists should study patients' feelings as well as their cells.
explanation: Put the poem into plain English. The speaker has looked at these cells so often that they are 'only shapes.' Then 'But' brings the turn: it's the speaker's own blood, a cell destroys something harmful, and the speaker thanks it out loud. Choice B covers the routine and the gratitude it turns into.

A.why: This only describes the comparisons in the opening lines. It skips the turn after 'But,' which is where the poem's meaning is. That is the usual poetry trap.

C.why: The first half is right, but the cell is doing its job by destroying 'a thing that would have harmed me.' The speaker feels grateful, not afraid.

D.why: This turns a private moment into a lesson for the whole field. The poem never makes that claim.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Clear pivot from routine cell-naming to personal gratitude; one step with subtlety of emotional significance.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Agnes, a museum curator who studies historical textiles, is examining a nineteenth-century quilt.

The catalog called it a utility quilt, and Agnes had expected to spend ten minutes on it. The cottons were cheap mill prints, faded unevenly; the batting had shifted into lumps. But turning back a corner, she found the maker had worked a second pattern into the quilting itself, a vine of tiny stitches running unseen beneath the patchwork from one edge to the other. Agnes pulled her chair closer. The afternoon went, and then the light, and she did not reach for the next box.
choices: Agnes, who expected to dismiss a plain quilt quickly, becomes absorbed after finding its hidden craft.
Agnes, who expected to dismiss a plain quilt quickly, decides the rest of the catalog is also wrong.
Agnes observes that the quilt's cotton prints are inexpensive and have faded unevenly over time.
Agnes grows weary of the tedious work and puts off examining the rest of the museum's collection.
explanation: Agnes plans on 'ten minutes.' After 'But' she finds hidden stitching, pulls her chair closer, and works until dark. Choice A matches both the situation (a quilt she expected to rush through) and where her feeling goes (complete absorption).

B.why: The first half is right, but the text says nothing about the other catalog entries. This is the half-right answer. Read to the end of every choice.

C.why: This is a true detail from one sentence, but it is too narrow. It leaves out the discovery and Agnes's absorption, which the passage is about.

D.why: It's true that she doesn't open the next box, but this gives the wrong reason. She is absorbed, not tired. The tone is reversed.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Straightforward reversal: expected dismissal gives way to absorption when hidden craft is discovered.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Marcus, a labor economist, has returned with his father to the factory town where his father once worked.

In his papers Marcus had written about the town as a data point: a plant closure in 1994, a wage decline of eighteen percent over a decade, the out-migration of workers under thirty. The figures were correct, and he had been proud of them. Now, standing outside the shuttered gates, he listened to his father name each window (the paint shop, the loading bay, the break room where he had eaten lunch for twenty-six years), and Marcus felt, for the first time, how little his numbers had held.
choices: Visiting the plant with his father, Marcus realizes that his published wage figures were inaccurate.
Marcus recalls the specific statistics he once published about the town's plant closure and wages.
Visiting the plant with his father, Marcus sees how much his accurate statistics failed to capture.
Marcus returns to the town in order to gather fresh evidence for a new study of plant closures.
explanation: The text says outright that 'the figures were correct.' Listening to his father's memories, Marcus sees 'how little his numbers had held.' The numbers weren't wrong. They just left out the lives behind them. Choice C keeps both points: the statistics were accurate and they were not enough.

A.why: This is the half-right answer. The setting is right, but the text says 'the figures were correct.' Marcus is learning what his numbers left out, not that they were wrong.

B.why: This only covers the opening sentence. It leaves out the visit and what Marcus realizes, which the passage builds to.

D.why: This adds a reason for the trip that the text never gives. Nothing mentions a new study. He is there with his father.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Requires sophisticated understanding that 'correct' statistics can be comprehensively inadequate to capture human meaning.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Ines, a county nurse, is going from farm to farm offering vaccinations during a diphtheria outbreak.

By the ninth farmhouse Ines had stopped counting the miles. Her satchel had grown heavy with unused vials, and at three doors she had been turned away before she could speak. Still, at each gate she paused to straighten her collar, as if the next family might be the first to listen. At the Pruitt place a girl of six came out alone, held out her arm without being asked, and watched the needle with grave interest. Ines drove home in the dark, tired to the bone, and found she was humming.
choices: Though Ines's rounds are long and often met with refusal, one willing child leaves her quietly cheered at the end of the day.
Though Ines's rounds are long and often met with refusal, she keeps making them mainly to avoid disappointing the county doctor.
A young girl at the Pruitt farm accepts her vaccination calmly and holds out her arm before anyone has asked her to.
Ines grows bitter toward the families who turn her away and dreads each new gate she has to approach that day.
explanation: Follow Ines's feeling from start to end. The day is exhausting and discouraging (unused vials, three refusals), yet she keeps going with hope at every gate, and after the Pruitt girl's eager arm she drives home 'tired to the bone' and humming. Choice A covers both halves: the hard, rejected rounds and the lift that one receptive child gives her.

B.why: The first half matches A word for word, so you probably stopped reading there. The second half gives Ines a motive the text never mentions. No doctor appears, and nothing suggests she is working to avoid anyone's disapproval.

C.why: This is accurate, but it covers only one moment. It leaves out Ines, the long and discouraging day, and the way she feels at the end, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

D.why: This reverses the tone. Ines straightens her collar at each gate 'as if the next family might be the first to listen,' which is hope, not dread, and she ends the day humming, not bitter.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker recalls nights spent with a parent at a backyard telescope.

My father named them as he swung the tube:
Vega, Albireo, the smudge of Andromeda.
I wrote each name in a notebook by red light,
proud of the list, impatient for the next.
Now, years past his voice, I find the notebook
and see I never wrote down what I saw,
only what he called it. Tonight I go out
with no name in my head, and look.
choices: Finding an old notebook, the speaker realizes that as a child they collected the names of stars instead of seeing them, and resolves now simply to look.
Finding an old notebook, the speaker resolves to relearn the names of the stars that their father once pointed out to them through a telescope.
The speaker recalls feeling proud as a child while writing down the names of the stars that their father found and named through the telescope.
The speaker resents a father who moved through the night sky too quickly for a child to take in what the telescope was showing.
explanation: In plain English: as a child, the speaker eagerly listed every star name the father gave. As an adult, rereading the list, the speaker sees that it holds only labels and no record of what they actually saw, so tonight they go out 'with no name in my head, and look.' Choice A follows that whole movement, from collecting names, to realizing what was missed, to deciding to observe.

B.why: The opening fits, but the resolution is backwards. The speaker goes out deliberately 'with no name in my head.' The point is to stop relying on names, not to relearn them.

C.why: This describes only the first four lines, the childhood memory. It misses the turn at 'Now,' where the speaker reflects on that habit and changes it, and that turn is what the poem is about.

D.why: The poem blames no one, least of all the father. The impatience belongs to the child ('impatient for the next'), and the speaker never expresses resentment.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a memoir. The author recalls her first season as a volunteer at a bird-banding station.

I had expected the work to feel like science: tidy, numbered, remote. For the first weeks it did. I weighed each warbler in a plastic tube, read its wing length off a steel rule, and called the numbers to Dov, who wrote them down. However, one morning a chickadee I was holding stopped struggling and simply looked at me, its heart going so fast against my fingers that I lost count of it. I released it and forgot to call the weight. Dov said nothing, but after that he let me hold each bird a moment longer before I spoke.
choices: An encounter with one bird changes the author's sense of banding from detached measurement into something more personal and felt.
An encounter with one bird changes the author's sense of banding, leading her to doubt that its measurements are worth recording.
The author becomes so distracted by a chickadee's rapid heartbeat that she forgets to call out the bird's weight to Dov.
Dov begins letting the author hold each bird longer so that she will stop making careless mistakes in her recording.
explanation: The passage sets up an expectation ('tidy, numbered, remote') and then turns on 'However.' The chickadee's gaze and racing heart break that detachment, and Dov quietly makes room for the new feeling. Choice A names both the starting view and what it changes into, which is the arc of the whole passage.

B.why: The first half is correct, so it is easy to accept the whole choice. But the author never questions whether the data matter. Forgetting one weight is a lapse in a moving moment, not a judgment that measuring is pointless.

C.why: This is true, but it is a single incident. It leaves out the author's earlier expectations and the lasting change afterward, so it is too narrow for the main idea.

D.why: This gives Dov a motive the text never states. He 'said nothing' and let her hold each bird longer, which reads as respect for what she felt. Nothing suggests he was correcting her carelessness.

subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a short story. Marguerite, an archaeologist near the end of her career, is excavating an ancient well.

For thirty seasons Marguerite had wanted the great find: a hoard, an inscription, anything the journals would print. The well gave her potsherds, a bent nail, the jaw of a goat. On the last afternoon her trowel turned up a clay cup with a thumbprint pressed into the rim, small, perhaps a child's, set there before the clay was fired. She sat back on her heels for a long while. The journals would not want it. She wrapped it more carefully than anything she had ever found.
choices: Though her final dig yields nothing of the importance she long sought, Marguerite is deeply moved by a humble cup bearing one person's mark.
Though her final dig yields nothing of the importance she long sought, Marguerite expects the thumbprinted cup to finally win her recognition.
Marguerite is disappointed that her final excavation turns up only a clay cup, a bent nail, and other ordinary objects.
A small thumbprint pressed into a clay cup's rim suggests that the vessel may have been handled by a child before firing.
explanation: The opening establishes Marguerite's lifelong wish for a find the journals would print, and the well gives her nothing of the kind. The last sentences add it all up: she knows 'the journals would not want it,' yet she wraps the cup 'more carefully than anything she had ever found.' Choice A captures both the unmet ambition and what she feels about the cup.

B.why: The first half is right, but the second half contradicts the text, which says outright that 'the journals would not want it.' Marguerite treasures the cup for personal reasons, not for recognition.

C.why: This reverses the emotional direction of the ending. The cup does not disappoint her. She sits with it 'for a long while' and wraps it with more care than any other find.

D.why: This restates a detail about the cup accurately, but it leaves Marguerite out entirely. The passage is about what the cup means to her, so a statement about the object alone is too narrow.
